---
title: "Day 19 demo: a proton-transfer equilibrium workbench"
---

**Question:** can you predict a favoured proton-transfer direction from the
reactant and product acids, without confusing equilibrium with reaction speed?

Allow **8 minutes**: predict for 2, compare cases for 4, and explain for 2.
All numerical inputs and reacting species are supplied in the workbench.

```{=html}
<section class="chem-demo" id="day19" aria-label="Compatible aqueous pKa and proton-transfer equilibrium workbench">
<p>Enable JavaScript to select a proton donor and base and inspect the complete conjugate-pair reaction.</p>
</section>
<script src="../interactives/core.js"></script>
<script src="../interactives/applications.js"></script>
```

## Predict

For the reaction HA + B ⇌ A + BH, compare the conjugate-pair pKa values using

$$K\approx10^{pK_a(BH)-pK_a(HA)}.$$

Charges depend on the chosen pair; the actual charged formulas are displayed.
The supplied approximate aqueous acid pKa values are ethanoic acid **4.8**,
methylammonium **10.6**, phenol **10.0** and pyridinium **5.2**. A lower pKa
means a stronger acid within this compatible comparison.

Predict the result of ethanoic acid with methylamine before using the controls.

## Explore

1. Inspect all four species, not only the numerical constant.
2. Try **Equal pair**. Why does swapping a proton within the same conjugate-pair
   bookkeeping give K = 1?
3. Try **Reactant-favoured case** and identify the weaker acid on each side.
4. Make your own product-favoured comparison and check the net charge.

## Explain and check

Ethanoic acid plus methylamine gives a pKa difference of $10.6-4.8=5.8$, so
$K\approx6.3\times10^5$ toward ethanoate plus methylammonium. Phenol plus
pyridine gives $5.2-10.0=-4.8$, so $K\approx1.6\times10^{-5}$ and reactants
are favoured. Neither value specifies how rapidly equilibrium is approached.

## Model limits

The values are approximate and used under a common aqueous comparison.
Standard-state, activity, solvent and temperature conventions must be
compatible when transferring this calculation to other datasets. K alone
also does not give the final composition without starting amounts and an
appropriate equilibrium model. No equilibrium solver or laboratory protocol
is implied. Review the [local acid–base explanation](../acids-bases/exercise.qmd).
